IHC working on policy to rotate judges to other provinces. ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) administration has started working on a policy for rotation of judges of the subordinate judiciary to other provinces, a long-awaited demand of the capital’s legal fraternity that was accepted in principle by the National Judicial Policy Making Committee (NJPMC). Informed sources said several proposals were being considered to determine the modalities for implementing the inter-provincial rotation of judges of Islamabad’s district judiciary. One proposal under consideration is that judicial officers posted to other provinces should preferably be sent to the province from where they originally belong. The Islamabad judiciary comprises officers who joined the service through different modes, including initial appointments, absorption and deputation, and judicial officers from all four provinces are currently serving in the capital. The sources said there were around 60 judicial officers in the Islamabad judiciary, and the authorities were considering whether all of them, 50pc of them or one-third should be rotated to other provinces. Another issue under consideration is whether the rotation should cover all tiers of the subordinate judiciary — civil judges, senior civil judges, additional district and sessions judges and district and sessions judges — or be limited to certain categories. “Whatever formula is adopted, one thing is clear: the equal number of judges sent from Islamabad will be brought in from the provinces to maintain the strength of the district judiciary,” a legal expert familiar with the proposed mechanism said. The proposed policy follows a longstanding demand by Islamabad’s lawyers for giving the district judiciary of the federal capital the same opportunity for inter-provincial transfers and rotations available to judges in the provinces. In May, the Islamabad High Court Bar Association formally demanded a uniform transfer and rotation policy for the district judiciary. The NJPMC subsequently accepted the demand in principle and decided to introduce inter-provincial rotation of Islamabad’s subordinate judiciary. The move came after years of calls from the legal fraternity for greater institutional balance in the capital’s district courts. The issue has gained further significance following the transfer of three IHC judges to the Lahore, Peshawar and Sindh high courts earlier this year. Bar bodies had subsequently called for a structured and periodic rotation mechanism for judges rather than selective transfers. The concept of rotating Islamabad’s lower court judges is not new. In 2018, the federal government had proposed amendments to the Islamabad Judicial Service Rules to enable subordinate court judges to be sent on deputation to other provinces, while noting that the existing rules did not provide for such transfers. The proposed mechanism has, however, also generated apprehensions among some judicial officers. Concerns have been expressed that frequent movement between Islamabad and other provinces could expose judges to new forms of professional pressure, including attempts by lawyers to influence judicial decisions or pressure judges considered “non-cooperative”. The authorities are therefore faced with the task of devising a transparent and uniform mechanism that provides for inter-provincial exposure and rotation while safeguarding judicial independence and ensuring that the strength of Islamabad’s district judiciary remains intact. The final policy is expected to settle the number and categories of judges to be rotated, the duration of their postings and the procedure for replacing them with judicial officers from other provinces. Published in Dawn, September 23rd, 2026

Asian Development Bank keeps Pakistan's growth forecast at 3.7pc. ISLAMABAD: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) on Wednesday forecast Pakistan’s economic growth rate at 3.7 per cent — lower than the 4pc budget target — and inflation at 8.3pc — higher than the official estimate of 7pc for the current fiscal year — amid downside risks stemming from the conflict in the Middle East. “Pakistan’s gross domestic product growth is projected to remain at 3.7pc in FY2027”, the Manila-based lending agency said in its Asian Development Outlook September episode. In its latest outlook, ADB has maintained its July forecast of 3.7pc. It had earlier projected a 4.5pc growth rate for the current fiscal year in its April 2026 forecast. “Average inflation is projected to rise to 8.3pc in FY27, above the central bank’s medium-term target range of 5pc–7pc, as elevated energy, logistics, and agricultural input costs continue to affect domestic prices”, it added. The bank warned that the economic outlook was subject to significant downside risks. An escalation of the Middle East conflict could increase energy import costs, intensify inflation, and disrupt labour markets in Gulf economies, affecting workers’ remittances. “The reintroduction of austerity measures by the Pakistan government could also weigh on domestic demand and economic activity, particularly if expenditure restraint is more pronounced than anticipated, posing an additional downside risk to the economic outlook”, the ADB noted. It also highlighted other risks including tighter global financing conditions, shortfalls in tax revenue, weather-related agricultural shocks, and delays in energy-sector and state-owned enterprise reforms. The ADB emphasised consistent implementation of reforms as critical to reinforcing fiscal and external stability and sustaining investor confidence. It noted that Pakistan’s economic performance continued to strengthen in fiscal year 2026 (FY26, ended 30 June 2026), with growth accelerating to 3.7pc from 3.2pc in FY25. The expansion was broad-based, supported by resilient services, a rebound in manufacturing, recovery in agriculture, and stronger private investment, although the Middle East conflict slowed economic activity in the final quarter of the fiscal year. Sustained implementation of economic reforms, improved external buffers, renewed access to international capital markets, and recent sovereign credit rating upgrades are expected to support investor confidence and private investment. However, elevated energy prices and continued external uncertainty, including lingering effects of the Middle East conflict, are expected to constrain further acceleration in growth. “Pakistan’s economy has made progress in strengthening macroeconomic stability over the past two years, with stronger growth, improved external buffers, restored market confidence, and sovereign credit rating upgrades reflecting the benefits of sustained reforms”, said ADB Country Director for Pakistan Emma Fan. “Maintaining reform momentum will be critical to unlock higher private investment, strengthen resilience to external shocks, and achieve stronger and more inclusive growth.“ Growth in FY26 was supported by expansion in manufacturing and services. Agriculture grew by 2.9pc, despite flood-related losses to major crops, while private investment increased by 8.6pc amid lower borrowing costs and improved business confidence, ADB said. Fiscal consolidation continued during FY26. Gross international reserves increased, strengthening external resilience. Pakistan’s sovereign credit ratings were upgraded by S&P in July 2026 and Moody’s in August 2026, reflecting improved macroeconomic stability, stronger external buffers, and continued reform implementation. Pakistan also regained access to international capital markets through Eurobond and Panda bond issuances in April and May 2026. Inflation averaged 7.1pc in FY26, compared with 4.5pc in FY25, as rising food prices and higher global oil prices intensified price pressures during the second half of the year.

With reconstruction stalled, Gazans shelter in buildings at risk of collapse. In her Gaza City apartment, Heba Arafat walks uphill across a living room slanted at a steep angle after Israeli airstrikes caused the building’s foundations to collapse, leaving the entire structure tilted. Like thousands of people in Gaza, Arafat chose to risk living in an apartment building damaged during nearly three years of Israel’s military actions, with countless Israeli airstrikes on the Palestinian territory. “We were forced to live here because we had nowhere else to go. All of our homes were destroyed, our land was razed and we have nothing left,” said Arafat, 47. People walk at a site destroyed during the Israeli offensive, in Beit Lahiya, in the northern Gaza Strip, on August 18, 2026. — Reuters According to the UN, 84 per cent of all structures in Gaza had been damaged or destroyed by October 2025, and Gaza’s civil defence says 2,000 buildings across the territory are at risk of collapse. Last week, 21 people, including 12 children, died in Gaza City after a six-storey building that local authorities said had been hit repeatedly by Israeli airstrikes collapsed. Israel denied having struck the building. Arafat lives with her six daughters and husband in their old apartment building in Gaza City’s Al-Shati Refugee Camp, which they left at the height of the conflict that began in October 2023 with Hamas’s massive attack on Israel. The family returned after an October 2025 ceasefire, which has reduced but not ended Israeli strikes. They found that their four-storey building, in which 30 people now live, had collapsed inward at the ground floor, the result, she said, of an Israeli ground operation in the area. Like most buildings in Gaza City, the windows were blown away by blasts, with makeshift bedsheets spread across the frames providing little privacy. As she spoke, Arafat illustrated her building’s slant by leaving a water bottle sideways on the floor, only for it to quickly roll away to the other end of the room. While no territory-wide estimate exists, Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN humanitarian coordinator for the Palestinian territories, said last week that people across Gaza were living in “hundreds of damaged and unsafe shelters”. ‘Where can we go?’ “Where can we go? Even though this house is dangerous,” Arafat said. “We have been terrified ever since we heard about houses collapsing. The danger has become even greater” than we thought it would be. Gaza City municipal staff patrol the streets to identify buildings at risk of collapse and mark them with stencils. A displaced Palestinian man stands on the balcony of a heavily damaged building still used as shelter in Khan Yunis in the southern Gaza Strip on September 19, 2026. — AFP “These homes pose a genuine threat to the lives of the displaced persons sheltering inside them, as well as to residents in the vicinity and those in nearby displacement camps,” said Hosni Muhanna, a Gaza City spokesman. But Muhanna knows that people are likely to remain in these buildings for lack of better options. “Thousands of displaced people are forced to seek shelter in these dilapidated buildings which are on the verge of collapse to escape the hardships of displacement camps that offer no protection against the summer heat or winter cold.” Most residents of Gaza were displaced at least once during the conflict, and many of them remain in enormous camps for the displaced, in tents provided by humanitarian organisations or in improvised shelters. Stalled reconstruction With diseases such as the skin infection impetigo rampaging through certain camps due to the lack of waste disposal and general overcrowding, many Gaza residents have found it safer to take the risks of moving into the damaged buildings. And with Gaza’s economy in tatters, many remain dependent on aid, which Israel has allowed into Gaza with restrictions since the declaration of the US-brokered ceasefire in October 2025. A displaced Palestinian man stands on the balcony of a heavily damaged building still used as shelter in Khan Yunis in the southern Gaza Strip on September 19, 2026. — AFP But Israel has kept carrying out airstrikes, and has restricted the entry of a range of equipment that it says could also have military use, but which Gazans and international NGOs say are needed for the territory’s vast reconstruction needs. These can include large machinery needed to clear rubble from the site of destroyed buildings, or spare parts and lubricants needed to keep other tools running, UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric said in August. With the ceasefire process stalled for months, reconstruction efforts planned under the ceasefire have yet to begin. According to a joint assessment published by the UN, World Bank and European Union in April, Gaza will require $71.4 billion in recovery and reconstruction spending over the next decade. “We’re afraid a wall or the roof might fall on us, so we huddle together, afraid that one of us might get hurt,” Arafat said.

Leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly will find an organisation in need of revival. UN diplomacy aimed at halting wars and easing civilian suffering remains paralysed, while funding cuts have weakened UN capacity. States have one eye to the future as they prepare to appoint a new Secretary-General. Why does it matter? The UN remains the only universal forum for global cooperation on war and peace, even as the international order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope the next Secretary-General can help the organisation dispel its malaise and forge a new direction. What should be done? A new Secretary-General cannot resolve the world’s crises overnight, but this person should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capabilities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. I. Overview When world leaders last met at the UN General Assembly in September 2025, the organisation was in disarray, reeling from U.S. aid freezes and major-power disputes. A year on, the organisation remains trapped in an open-ended crisis, even after an additional round of cost cutting and other reforms. Under the Trump administration, the U.S. has morphed from a flawed champion of the international legal order into an overt scofflaw. While the U.S. has not repudiated the multilateral system anchored by the UN, it has done great damage to the organisation, insisting on shrinking multilateral peace operations, slow-rolling funding and tried to impose its ideological agenda. The Security Council continues to be a forum for hashing out big-power differences – with the U.S., Russia and China coming to agreement on second-tier files. But as regards the most salient peace and security challenges today – the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, as well as Ukraine and Sudan – the UN is notable mainly for being stuck. The next Secretary-General cannot cure all that ails the UN, but creative diplomacy could be useful in putting its still considerable capacity to work. If the overall mood at the UN is one of drifting toward perdition, it is partly because everyone is waiting for change at the top of the system. Secretary-General António Guterres will complete his term at the end of December. A small batch of candidates – eight, at the time of writing – have been publicly and privately lobbying throughout the year to replace him. Most have been cautious in their campaigning, to avoid offending the major powers that dominate the selection process. UN insiders are watching with mixed feelings. Some hope that the next Secretary-General can bring new energy to the organisation and, assuming Washington is amenable, restore a measure of political relevance and financial stability. Others worry that the U.S., China and Russia will connive to choose a weak candidate firmly under their control and that the Trump administration will force the next UN chief to make even more radical cuts throughout the institution. The selection process has at least focused minds on what the UN, multilateral cooperation and international law exist to achieve. Many member states have emphasised that they would like to see the incoming Secretary-General do more to promote conflict prevention and resolution, which Guterres has sometimes given short shrift while pursuing other goals, such as international cooperation on artificial intelligence. Guterres no doubt felt that he had little to gain by focusing on geopolitical crises given the lack of consensus among the big powers. But there is now a widespread sense that the UN cannot pretend to be a useful platform for discussions of far-reaching issues like AI if governments do not believe that it can deliver on its core, UN Charter-defined purpose of maintaining peace and security. The crises of the last twelve months have also offered reminders of the extent to which the UN still offers a necessary if imperfect scaffolding for international cooperation. The Trump administration has grudgingly turned to the Security Council to endorse its conflict management efforts in Haiti and Gaza. Faced with the fallout of the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, such as closure of the Strait of Hormuz, governments around the world have stressed the importance of international legal principles including the prohibition of aggressive war, rules protecting civilians and civilian objects in conflict, and freedom of navigation. Though the UN has had a vanishingly small voice in diplomacy aimed at ending the Middle East war, both U.S. and Iranian officials have acknowledged that the Security Council should play some role – if only a ministerial one – in any peace deal. The UN ... remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors ... can handle. These are small consolations, but at a moment in which the U.S. and Russia are learning the limits of hard power in the Middle East and Ukraine, there is still space to reiterate the case for diplomacy, cooperation and respect for law. The next UN Secretary-General can make it. While it is foolish to expect a single administrator, however senior, to save the world, many small and midsize UN member states, as well as many major-power officials, are ready to heed a call to reinforce the lapsing international legal order. The UN also remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors – including the flailing U.S.-backed Board of Peace – can handle. It is possible that new leadership at the UN can give the organisation as a whole, and its peace and security pillar in particular, a new strategic direction. But amid deadly violence, regional rifts and institutional headaches, it is a near certainty that UN crisis management will continue to involve a great deal of firefighting and muddling through. This briefing, based on Crisis Group’s research at the UN and in the countries concerned, offers a guide to some of the most urgent issues. II. The Year in Review: Trends in UN Diplomacy The UN spent much of the past year adapting to a more assertive and transactional U.S. administration. Alongside long-running crises in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, the latest U.S.-Israeli war with Iran placed additional strain on Council diplomacy and the UN-backed international order. 1 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°14, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Power , 8 July 2026. Meanwhile, the UN’s multi-year liquidity crisis worsened, compounded by the U.S. aid cuts, disrupting operations at headquarters in New York and in the field. Steep reductions in voluntary contributions to UN humanitarian agencies forced the organisation to make difficult choices with its assistance, leaving many civilians affected by armed conflict with little support. Debates over the UN’s future simmered as member states began their search for the next Secretary-General. A year after Donald Trump’s return to the White House, the organisation was no longer in shock but adjusting to a new normal. A. Crisis Management and UN Diplomacy 1. The Security Council A year ago, Crisis Group observed that U.S. diplomacy at the Security Council under the newly installed Trump administration had lacked a clear direction. 2 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°13, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2025-2026 , 9 September 2025. The arrival of U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz in New York on the eve of the 2025 UN General Assembly marked the beginning of a more purposeful, and often determined, U.S. approach in the Council. Together with Panama, the U.S. secured Council authorisation for a new Gang Suppression Force for Haiti shortly after Waltz’s arrival, along with a UN logistics office to defray some of the Force’s costs (see Section III.4). 3 “ Haiti: Vote on a Draft Resolution Authorizing a ‘Gang Suppression Force’ and a UN Support Office* ”, Security Council Report, 30 September 2025; Daniel Forti, “ New Force to Battle Haiti’s Gangs Gets Security Council Blessing ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 1 October 2025; Crisis Group Latin America & Caribbean Report N°110, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , 15 December 2025. Less than two months later, the Trump administration – backed by its regional partners and Palestine – persuaded the Council to endorse its ceasefire plan for Gaza and establish the vaguely defined Board of Peace. 4 “Resolution 2803”, UNSC S/RES/2803, 17 November 2025; Daniel Forti, Richard Gowan and Max Rodenbeck, “ What to Look for as the Gaza Peace Plan Comes to the UN Security Council ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 November 2025. In both cases, the Council agreed to arrangements that concentrated decision-making authority in Washington and minimised the UN’s political and operational roles. With UN diplomacy on the war in Gaza lowered to a simmer (see Section III.3), the U.S.-Iran conflict became the Council’s defining crisis of the past year. Major-power tensions over Iran were already high at the UN prior to the outbreak of hostilities at the end of February. After the breakdown of nuclear diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran in 2025 and the twelve-day campaign launched by Israel (and joined by the U.S.) against Iran in June, France, Germany and the UK – three of the participants in the 2015 nuclear deal, or Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action – decided to reimpose “snapback” sanctions on Tehran that were otherwise set to expire that October. 5 Naysan Rafati and Daniel Forti, “ Iran Sanctions Snapback at the UN ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 25 August 2026. Beijing and Moscow rejected the legality of the reimposed UN sanctions, and in protest, they have obstructed business in all of the Council’s sanctions committees and thematic working groups since 2026 began. 6 China and Russia have blocked the appointment of the chairs and vice chairs of all subsidiary bodies, which require Council unanimity according to the body’s informal working methods. The chairs and vice chairs are responsible for leading each body’s meetings, briefing the Council on behalf of each body and managing its workflow. For more, see “ In Hindsight: A Second Year of Delays in the Allocation of Subsidiary Body Chairs ”, Security Council Report, 1 July 2026; Letter from the Security Council’s ten elected members , UNSC S/2026/636, 30 July 2026. Tensions in the Council gradually escalated after the U.S. and Israel once again attacked Iran on 28 February. China and Russia sharply criticised the two states during the Council’s first emergency meeting on the war. But even so they allowed passage of a Bahrain-led resolution condemning Iran’s retaliatory fire at its Gulf Arab neighbours days later, abstaining instead of vetoing it. Their posture suggested that preserving relations with the Gulf states was a higher priority than blocking a one-sided resolution that had no teeth. 7 Beijing and Moscow abstained from the vote. Russia also submitted a separate counter-resolution discussing the war’s root causes that got too few votes to be adopted. See “ Resolution 2817 ”, UNSC S/RES/2817, 11 March 2026. Their stances gradually hardened, however, as Washington pressed the Security Council to consider more coercive measures against Tehran. In early April, the Gulf states and the U.S. tabled a resolution for the Council to endorse a vaguely defined multinational naval coalition that would be tasked with reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Moscow and Beijing vetoed the text despite intense lobbying by Gulf capitals, arguing that the resolution would have given the U.S. open-ended authorisation to escalate its campaign. 8 The vote took place hours after U.S. President Donald Trump shared a social media message threatening to annihilate Iran. During its explanation of vote, Russia invoked the Security Council’s 2011 open-ended authorisation of NATO-led military action in Libya as a comparison to the proposed Gulf-U.S. initiative. Despite finding over 138 co-sponsors, the U.S. and Bahrain did not submit the text for a vote, as they could not secure the support of Russia and China. Council diplomacy on the file has since stalled. Complex and sometimes volatile relations among the U.S., China, and Russia continue to shape the boundaries of Council diplomacy beyond the Gulf. After the reversal of U.S. Ukraine policy in early 2025, when the Trump administration stopped sending arms to Kyiv to resist Russia’s all-out invasion, Moscow may have expected Washington to press the Ukrainian government to make concessions in negotiations to end the fighting. Instead, U.S. statements in the Security Council have criticised Russia’s full-scale invasion and called on the Kremlin to agree to an immediate ceasefire. 9 Remarks by the United States, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10166th Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10166, 8 June 2026. More often than not, U.S. and Russian diplomats have sparred over UN responses to crises in the Middle East and Africa. By contrast, Washington and Beijing have shown willingness to strike occasional deals in the Security Council. Though they frequently clash, recent Council action has depended on a degree of cooperation between these geopolitical rivals. In September 2025, the U.S. agreed to pay nearly $680 million to the UN peacekeeping budget and drop its objections to China becoming penholder on the Council’s Afghanistan file in exchange for Beijing’s support for the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. 10 Daniel Forti and Richard Gowan, “ Reading the Signals of China’s U.N. Unusually, several elected members have found themselves directly implicated in issues before the Council in 2026 to date. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Somalia sought to preserve ties with the U.S. while influencing Council discussions on conflicts in their own countries. 16 Kinshasa has used its elected term on the Security Council to raise the profile of the conflict in the eastern DRC, while Mogadishu has sought to end the Council’s engagement with the war in Somalia. The Secretary-General Secretary-General Guterres has spent much of his final year in office trying to forestall the UN’s urgent financial crisis (discussed below), complete reforms under the UN80 initiative that he launched in 2025 and defend the UN Charter in response to violations by two permanent members, Russia and the U.S. 21 The UN80 initiative, launched by Guterres in March 2025, is premised on three separate reform processes. The first is premised on budget cuts and cost savings at the UN Secretariat; the second features a review of all inter-governmental mandates; and the third is anchored in proposals for larger institutional reforms (including proposals to merge different UN agencies and offices). “ UN80 Initiative ”, UN, August 2026. Neither Moscow nor Washington is eager to engage with him personally, curtailing his opportunities to pursue new diplomatic efforts. But the Secretary-General’s cautious outlook toward UN-led conflict management has left many diplomats and officials searching for a successor who will put the organisation’s work on peace and security front and centre. The Secretary-General’s limited influence over the past year has not always been due to a lack of initiative. Shortly after the resumption of hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, Guterres appealed for creating a humanitarian corridor to permit the passage of fuel and fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz, established a UN mechanism modelled on the Black Sea Grain Initiative to facilitate these efforts and appointed a personal envoy to boost the UN’s diplomatic response. 22 “ Note to Correspondents: on the Strait of Hormuz ”, UN, 27 March 2026. His focus on the war’s global consequences won plaudits but failed to have meaningful impact, as neither the Gulf states nor the U.S. showed serious interest in reopening the strait, except in full and without condition. The initiative has faded from memory even as the war has reignited and traffic through the waterway remains constrained. 23 Guterres shared a brief update about the UN mechanism at a 24 August press conference. See “ Secretary-General’s Press Encounter – On the United Nations’ Efforts to Uphold Navigational Rights and Freedoms ”, Office of the UN Secretary-General, 24 August 2026. Elsewhere, Guterres has deployed his dwindling political capital selectively. At the end of July, he travelled to Cyprus to revive his long-running mediation between Greek and Turkish Cypriots. He also made personal appeals to Sudan’s belligerents in support of a proposed humanitarian ceasefire in Darfur. The Secretary-General continued to press for Security Council reform, including at a high-level summit convened by France and Kenya in May, and in August he released a long-awaited review of UN peace operations mandated by the 2024 Pact for the Future (see Section III.9). 24 “ Review on the future of all forms of United Nations Peace Operations ”, UNGA A/80/798 – UNSC S/2026/600, 22 July 2026. Yet meaningful progress on these and other such priorities has eluded him. B. UN Reform The UN’s financial outlook has deteriorated sharply over the past year, largely due to Washington’s failure to pay its fair share. Since President Trump returned to office, the U.S. has ponied up only a portion of the nearly $4 billion in dues it owes the organisation. 25 In late August, the U.S. agreed to make a payment of $725 million to the UN regular budget, an amount reportedly calculated by Washington to avoid losing its vote in the General Assembly under Article 19 of the UN Charter. The U.S. is not the only member state withholding its obligatory dues, even if it is the largest and has accumulated the most arrears. China has regularly delayed its annual payments to the UN regular budget – in 2026 paying only at the beginning of September – though it traditionally does not accumulate arrears. C. The Search for a New Secretary-General The process of choosing Guterres’ successor, which began in November 2025, is approaching a crescendo. Members of the Security Council held their first straw poll at the end of July, and they will continue to take these informal soundings until one candidate receives at least nine votes from the fifteen-member body with no objection from any of the five permanent members. Eight candidates are in the running. Ten Challenges for the UN Even as the UN is mired in interlocking difficulties, the organisation can still contribute to conflict resolution and crisis management in many domains. The following list features countries and issue areas where the UN confronts either major challenges or opportunities in the year ahead. It is intended to demonstrate the myriad factors affecting how the UN and its member states respond to conflicts and emergencies around the world. The list is not exhaustive, however, and it excludes cases that Crisis Group has highlighted elsewhere or in years past, such as Afghanistan, the DRC, South Sudan, Ukraine and others. 1. Continuing UN engagement in southern Lebanon In August 2025, the U.S. and Israel strong-armed the Security Council into shutting down the UN peacekeeping mission in southern Lebanon (UNIFIL) – first established in 1978 and significantly upgraded by Resolution 1701 twenty years ago – by the end of 2026 (though the phased withdrawal of troops will extend considerably past 31 December). 50 “ Resolution 2790 ”, UNSC S/RES/2790, 28 August 2025. While questions about southern Lebanon have long vexed the Council, the latest conflagration between Israel and Hizbollah raises the stakes even higher. 51 Heiko Wimmen and David Wood, “ Entrenching a Meaningful Israel-Lebanon Ceasefire ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 19 June 2026. The danger is now that the UN will terminate its 48-year blue helmet operation without clarity on what kind of international presence, if any, might follow. Much will now depend on the trajectory of U.S.-backed negotiations between Israel and Lebanon, which to date have failed to produce a viable security arrangement. The two states signed a “framework agreement” on 26 June, under which the Lebanese army is to assert control of “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon, ensuring that Hizbollah no longer has a military footprint in these areas. 52 “ Trilateral Framework Between the United States of America, the State of Israel and the Republic of Lebanon ”, U.S. Department of State, 26 June 2026. Yet the scheme, which is meant to “serve as the mechanism for phased and verified (Israeli) redeployments”, has already run into trouble. 53 Ibid. Lebanon complains that Israel has kept attacking Lebanese territory, including with lethal airstrikes and the systematic destruction of villages, and authorised “pilot zones” only in areas that it never occupied. Israeli officials, for their part, make Hizbollah’s full disarmament a condition for the Israeli army’s withdrawal. 54 Maayan Lubell and Maya Gebeily, “ After US criticism, Israel ties Lebanon withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament ”, Reuters, 13 August 2026. Beirut officially outlawed Hizbollah’s military activities in March, but, in practice, it cannot risk trying to compel the group to disarm. 55 Lebanese political and military leaders have resisted calls to deploy the Lebanese army to confront Hizbollah by force. They fear that such a move could trigger disastrous domestic consequences, such as the military fracturing along sectarian lines. Crisis Group Middle East Briefing N°94, Containing Domestic Tensions in War-hit Lebanon , 27 February 2025. See also Michael Young, “ Pushing Beirut into an armed conflict with Hezbollah is insane ”, Diwan (blog), Carnegie Middle East Center, 14 May 2026. Even if the terms of the deal were to be spelled out more precisely, the belligerents would almost certainly refuse to sign up to the underlying bargain. Hizbollah rejects the direct Israel-Lebanon negotiations outright, insisting that Lebanon entrust Iran, the group’s patron, with securing a full Israeli withdrawal as part of Tehran’s negotiations with Washington. 56 “ Hezbollah insists on linking Lebanon to Iran-U.S. negotiations ”, Asharq al-Awsat , 13 July 2026. Though Israel has participated in the trilateral talks with Lebanon and the U.S., it refuses to accept another arrangement like Resolution 1701, under which its troops withdrew from Lebanon after the 2006 war while Hizbollah remained under arms. Debates about a future international presence will also be shaped by U.S. and Israeli scepticism. Israel has long questioned the value of UNIFIL in helping Lebanon constrain Hizbollah, and it has shown little appetite for a replacement that might obstruct its own military operations. The U.S. does not oppose an international mission per se, but it is wary of replicating a UNIFIL model that it deems ineffective. 57 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and UN officials, Beirut, July 2026. The U.S. and its Israeli partners have long argued that UNIFIL has failed to deter Hizbollah military operations south of the Litani River (even if it has no mandate to confront the militant group by force) and is too expensive. For background, see David Wood, “ Helping UNIFIL Restore Stability in Southern Lebanon ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 August 2025. Washington has sidelined the monitoring mechanism attached to the November 2024 ceasefire, in which UNIFIL and France (the Council’s penholder on Lebanon) were represented. Instead, an annex of the June framework agreement provides for a U.S.-headed “military coordination group”, through which Israel and Lebanon will manage tasks that UNIFIL or a successor force might have helped tackle, including “deconfliction, verification and overall implementation”. 58 The parties did not officially release this annex to the framework agreement, but they have not challenged the authenticity of a text leaked to the media in late June. “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, L’Orient Today , 29 June 2026. Other Council members and Lebanon strongly favour retaining an international presence, having reluctantly agreed to UNIFIL’s termination at the end of 2026 to avoid a U.S. veto that would have abruptly ended the mission in August 2025. 59 “ UN Interim Force in Lebanon: Vote on Final Mandate Renewal and Drawdown* ”, Security Council Report, 28 August 2025; Jamie Prentis, “ Lebanese MPs urge UN to extend peacekeeping mission ”, The National , 24 July 2026. The framework agreement does not mention the UN or Security Council resolution 1701. The annex, however, proposes a future role for a “mutually agreed-upon third-party entity” to verify that non-state armed groups have been cleared from each “pilot zone”. 60 “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, op. cit. To date, Israeli, Lebanese and U.S. negotiators have struggled to flesh out what such verification would entail, making it difficult for interested nations to commit troops to a mission that might prove dangerous. Yet even if the framework agreement eventually falls by the wayside, any other attempt to reach a deal that would link Israel’s withdrawal from southern Lebanon and cessation of airstrikes with an end to Hizbollah attacks on Israel and disarmament of the group would in all likelihood hinge on some sort of third-party verification. International partners have begun debating options for a new multinational presence. In June, the Secretary-General proposed a follow-up UN mission involving both armed and unarmed troops. 61 The report, mandated by the Security Council in Resolution 2790, proposed three different deployment sizes: the largest option would entail 5,525 uniformed personnel, the middle one 3,370 and the lightest footprint approximately 1,980. See “ Letter dated 1 June 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, UNSC S/2026/453, 1 June 2026. France and Italy have also announced plans to create a new multinational coalition in southern Lebanon as a successor to UNIFIL. 62 “ Lebanon president welcomes French, Italian efforts to form coalition to succeed UNIFIL ”, Arab News , 26 June 2026. In parallel, the European Union is weighing a separate mission comprising civilian and military personnel to advise and possibly train Lebanese forces – outside southern Lebanon – in addition to the €180 million it has already committed to support the Lebanese army. 63 Louay Faour, “ European powers seek greater role in south Lebanon’s post-war security architecture ”, The New Arab , 12 July 2026; Lili Bayer, “ EU diplomatic service proposes mission to train Lebanese forces, documents show ”, Reuters, 24 June 2026;“ European Peace Facility: Council adopts EUR 100 million assistance measure in support of the Lebanese Armed Forces ”, press release, Council of the EU, 4 June 2026. Any new multinational mission would have no choice but to work alongside the Lebanese-Israeli-U.S. security arrangement, even if that is not fully defined. Any new multinational mission would have no choice but to work alongside the Lebanese-Israeli-U.S. security arrangement, even if that is not fully defined. States wishing to participate in a mission would almost certainly demand Security Council authorisation prior to sending troops to southern Lebanon so as to guarantee their legal and political protection. Given U.S. veto power, Washington’s support on the Council remains indispensable, meaning that UN members cannot circumvent the trilateral mechanism championed by the Trump administration. Between now and the end of December, diplomats should monitor the evolution of security arrangements on the ground in southern Lebanon, while seeking to work out with Washington what kind of international deployment, if any, would be beneficial to Lebanon and its stability. It is unlikely that any security arrangement, whether the June framework agreement and/or some future deal, will either fully disarm Hizbollah or completely dissuade Israel from conducting military operations in Lebanon. But withdrawing UNIFIL, with no immediate successor in place, could leave a vacuum that makes an already tense situation even more volatile. By inheriting UNIFIL’s most valuable functions – in particular, monitoring and on-the-ground deconfliction – a new multinational mission could set up a guardrail against fresh escalation. Ideally, that force would eventually assume other roles in bolstering a sustainable security arrangement for southern Lebanon that becomes durable enough to stand on its own feet. 2. Adapting the UN’s political strategy for Sudan The UN continues to be on the margins of diplomacy aimed at halting Sudan’s devastating civil war. Secretary-General Guterres’ appointment of Pekka Haavisto as the new UN envoy in February has offered the organisation an opportunity to refresh its approach. Ramtane Lamamra – the UN’s previous diplomatic lead – struggled to find a bridge between the main warring parties, the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), or to coordinate the array of mediators working to resolve the conflict. The UN has had varying degrees of success in securing local deals over aid access, and it continues to prepare for a possible role in overseeing aspects of a mooted ceasefire. 64 See the Sudan entry in Crisis Group Briefing, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2025-2026 , op. cit. It is hard to see the UN leading efforts to stop the war, given the number of powerful foreign states backing the belligerents, but it should use the coming months to support other diplomatic tracks and raise global awareness of the urgent need to end the fighting. 65 “ Sudan: Closed Consultations ”, Security Council Report, 17 April 2026. Nearly eighteen months ago, UN officials acknowledged that Sudan’s plight had become the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe. 66 “ UN Sudan Annual Results Report 2024 ”, UN Sudan, 4 June 2025. Conditions have only deteriorated since then. An independent UN panel determined that mass killings, rapes and other atrocities committed by the RSF in October 2025 in El Fasher, Darfur – the city that hosted the headquarters of the former UN peacekeeping operation UNAMID – were “indicators of a genocidal path”. 67 “ Sudan: Hallmarks of Genocide in El Fasher - Report of the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan ”, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), UN Doc A/HRC/61/77, 19 February 2026. Diplomats and UN officials alike are sounding the alarm about similar risks in El-Obeid, North Kordofan. 68 “ Sudan: Imminent offensive on El Obeid must be halted – Türk warns of catastrophic impact on civilians ”, press release, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, 18 June 2026; “ Joint Statement of G7 Foreign Ministers on El Obeid, Sudan ”, U.S. Department of State, July 2026; “ Security Council Press Statement on Sudan (SC/16392) ”, UN Security Council, 20 June 2026. The two warring sides and their outside backers still believe there is more to gain from fighting than from negotiations. As matters stand, the country is in effect partitioned between the army and the RSF. 69 Crisis Group Africa Report N°211, Divided Sudan, Elusive Peace , 13 April 2026. To date, political negotiations have yielded few results. Much of the diplomatic focus has fallen on the Quad, a platform involving the U.S. and the three Arab powers with the most sway over the conflict parties – Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Its September 2025 roadmap, however, has won over neither belligerent, while Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, at loggerheads in conflict settings from Libya to Yemen, are doubling down on backing the army and RSF, respectively, stymying agreement within the Quad about what to do. 70 “ Joint Statement on Restoring Peace and Security in Sudan ”, U.S. Department of State, 12 September 2025; Comfort Ero and Alan Boswell, “ Latest Sudan Conference Shows Diplomacy is Backsliding ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 17 April 2026. In parallel, the UN is working alongside the African Union (AU), the EU, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), a Horn of Africa body, and the Arab League to support Sudanese-led civilian political dialogues as part of a nascent diplomatic track called the Quintet; these mediators convened a meeting in Berlin in April and another in Addis Ababa two months later. 71 “ Sudan: Quintet Joint Statement on de-escalation of the conflict in Sudan ”, European External Action Service, 11 February 2026; “ Quintet Statement on Ongoing Consultations with Sudanese Political Actors ”, African Union, 6 June 2026. Sudanese participants cannot agree on how to move forward with the talks, however. Having completed an initial tour of Sudan and the region, Haavisto can begin revising the UN’s diplomatic strategy. 72 “ Pekka Haavisto (Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Sudan) on the situation in the country – Press Conference ”, Office of the UN Spokesperson, 25 June 2026. He will need to reassure all parties that the UN will be an independent, impartial counterpart, even though the army-led government is the legally recognised one in New York. Haavisto needs to build rapport with others across Sudan’s fragmented political spectrum, including armed, political and civil players that are enlisted in the war, on one side or the other, or are non-aligned, as well as the various African, Arab and other countries directly involved in the conflict in one way or another. He will also need to reach out to the RSF, even if its deeds have earned it widespread and deserved condemnation. Lamamra struggled to maintain this balance, with critics seeing him as weighting his engagements too heavily toward the army-led authorities and its allies. 73 Crisis Group interviews, opposition political figures; RSF officials and allies, October-November 2025. Haavisto now has a chance for a reset. Haavisto should also strengthen the UN’s contributions within the Quintet. He could begin by stepping up outreach to various civilian groups between official Quintet meetings, with a view to mending fences between them. He could also help institute more consistent interactions between the Quintet and the army-led government, which has so far proven reluctant to get involved with a political process that is independent of its authority and takes place outside the country. 74 “ Quintet Statement Ahead of Visit to Khartoum, the Republic of Sudan, 8-10 September ”, Delegation of the European Union to the African Union, 8 September 2026. The army is instead pursuing its own “national dialogue” inside Sudan, which few of its political or armed opponents look likely to join. Behind the scenes, the UN should ... search for opportunities to bolster and connect the two diplomatic coalitions driving peace efforts [in Sudan]. Behind the scenes, the UN should also search for opportunities to bolster and connect the two diplomatic coalitions driving peace efforts, neither of which appears to have momentum at present. One way forward would be for Haavisto to work closely with counterparts to quietly float proposals for how Sudan could be governed whenever the main belligerents and their outside patrons summon the political will to seek an end to the war. Haavisto could help communicate these proposals to Quad and Quintet members, the two warring parties, and Sudan’s other main political movements and figures. Though it is hard to imagine a breakthrough any time soon given the entrenched positions on both sides, the UN should separately continue planning for a possible role in backing humanitarian access and ceasefire arrangements between the army and RSF should regional support for peace efforts eventually rise. 75 The UN is not formal member of the Quad, but it has worked informally with the U.S. to scope out technicalities of a monitoring mechanism for the prospective humanitarian truce that was outlined in the Quad’s September 2025 roadmap. Lastly, the UN can redouble its efforts to draw world attention to Sudan’s war and humanitarian disaster, if nothing else to caution states about possible spillover. The next Secretary-General should make this task a priority – including by paying a solidarity visit to refugee camps in countries neighbouring Sudan – and also warn of the mounting risks to states in the Horn and Red Sea regions should the conflict fester. 76 Alan Boswell, “ As the Horn of Africa Nears Boiling Point, Time for Urgent Diplomacy ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 17 July 2026. The UN’s new leader should ensure that Haavisto and other UN envoys covering the Horn, central Africa and the Middle East remain in close contact in the hope of identifying opportunities to break the diplomatic deadlock among states in these areas. 3. Encouraging a role for the General Assembly in Gaza’s ceasefire Having repeatedly called for a ceasefire to halt Israel’s campaign against Hamas in Gaza from 2023-2025, the General Assembly has devoted little energy to discussing whether the mechanisms created to uphold it are working. The Security Council’s November 2025 endorsement of the Trump administration’s ceasefire plan in Resolution 2803 – including its highly unusual authorisation of a Trump-chaired Board of Peace to serve as Gaza’s transitional administration – has erected a de-facto firewall between the UN and the diplomatic apparatus overseeing the Palestinian enclave’s future, at least until the Board’s UN mandate expires at the end of 2027. 77 “Resolution 2803”, op. cit. With Gaza’s reconstruction at a virtual standstill and Israel tightening its grip on the territory, UN member states risk sitting idle as the U.S.-dominated Board veers further off course. 78 Crisis Group Middle East Report N°257, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , 24 August 2026. The Board’s backtracking on the terms of its own fifteen-point roadmap – which features a scheme for decommissioning Hamas’s weapons agreed to by Palestinian factions but opposed by Israel – is just one of many troubling developments. The Security Council is, unfortunately, unlikely to consider corrective action until the Board mandate’s 2027 sunset. In the interim, member states should at a minimum use the General Assembly to assess the Board’s performance and to catalyse diplomatic pressure for putting Gaza on track toward recovery and Palestinian statehood. The General Assembly was the hub of UN diplomatic activity on Gaza throughout the war, as both President Joe Biden and President Trump blocked the Security Council from taking meaningful action. UN members convened the Assembly’s Emergency Special Session on the Occupied Palestinian Territories (its dedicated format for discussing the broader conflict) on eight separate occasions, and they debated five failed Security Council resolutions. 79 The General Assembly debated the nine vetoed resolutions under a Liechtenstein-led veto initiative, established by the General Assembly in April 2022. For full list of General Assembly meetings convened under the veto initiative, see “ Living with the Veto ”, Security Council Report, 23 March 2026, p. 8. Member states adopted five major General Assembly decisions on various aspects of the conflict, including the New York Declaration of September 2025, which bolstered recognition of Palestinian statehood. 80 “ Admission of new Members to the United Nations ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/23, 10 May 2024; Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/24, 19 September 2024; “ Support for the mandate of the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/25, 16 December 2024; “ Protection of civilians and upholding legal and humanitarian obligations ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/27, 13 June 2025; “ Endorsement of the New York Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of the Question of Palestine and the Implementation of the Two-State Solution ”, UNGA A/80/L.1/Rev.1, 10 September 2025. Though these measures had limited impact on the ground, they signalled growing international opposition to the war’s trajectory. The Security Council’s endorsement of Trump’s ceasefire plan upended these dynamics. By agreeing to the U.S.-drafted resolution (unenthusiastically supported by regional mediators and the State of Palestine), they in effect outsourced all responsibility for Gaza’s recovery and governance to the Board of Peace. 81 In Resolution 2803, the Security Council authorises the Board of Peace to set up a transitional administration (supervising a Palestinian technocratic committee, as well as matters including reconstruction of Gaza, public services, humanitarian assistance, movement of persons in and out of the strip and the envisioned International Stabilisation Force. “Resolution 2803”, op. cit.; Forti, Gowan and Rodenbeck, “What to Look for as the Gaza Peace Plan Comes to the UN Security Council”, op. cit. Since then, the UN has been further isolated from diplomacy on Gaza. It neither participates in any of the Board’s structures nor has it been asked to help stand up the International Stabilisation Force envisaged by the Council-approved Trump plan. 82 Sigrid Kaag, who was the former UN Gaza Humanitarian Coordinator and the former UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, is a member of the Board of Peace’s Gaza Executive Board. The Board’s High Representative Nickolay Mladenov (a former UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process) has briefed the Council and submitted a report (as required by Resolution 2803), but the General Assembly has discussed the situation only once – indirectly – since November 2025. No member state has asked to reconvene the Emergency Special Session despite worsening conditions under the tenuous truce. 83 General Assembly Annual Event of the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People Commemorating the Nakba, 15 May 2026. The inattention seems particularly negligent given that Gaza’s circumstances are diverging from not only Resolution 2803, but also the array of General Assembly resolutions and international legal orders about Palestine. 84 Crisis Group Report, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , op. cit. The lack of tangible progress in nearly a year after reaching a purported ceasefire makes international actors complicit in a brutal status quo: Gaza’s people are in effect hostage to diplomatic forces outside their control. Unless something changes, they will remain under siege, subject to bombardment and denied a future until the Board of Peace decides that Hamas has met Israel’s demands. Washington would likely veto any Security Council action perceived to criticise Israel – which receives unconditional backing from the U.S. at the UN – or to cast doubt on the legitimacy and efficacy of Trump’s peace efforts. But that ought not to be a justification for inaction in the General Assembly or elsewhere. UN members should use the General Assembly to challenge the Board of Peace’s unhelpful domination of the diplomatic space. UN members should use the General Assembly to challenge the Board of Peace’s unhelpful domination of the diplomatic space. The next meeting of the Global Alliance for the Two-State Solution, scheduled for September, could kickstart that endeavour. Member states should also consider reconvening the General Assembly’s Tenth Emergency Special Session to continue these efforts beyond High-Level Week. In addition, members should use these forums to offer political backing to the Palestinian technocratic committee as a means of asserting Palestinian ownership of reconstruction. These platforms provide an opportunity to reaffirm the necessity of the UN-led aid distribution network in Gaza, which remains the most capable one in the strip. Members might also signal the costs they would impose on Israel (bilaterally or in regional blocs) if it continues to obstruct provisions of the ceasefire and prevent the Palestinian technocratic committee from working in Gaza. 85 For example, on 8 September the British foreign secretary announced a raft of measures against Israel responding to its construction of illegal settlements in the West Bank and obstruction of the Trump ceasefire plan for Gaza. See Ed Miliband, “ Foreign Secretary Oral Statement on Israel-Palestine ”, speech to UK Parliament, 8 September 2026. For background, see Crisis Group Report, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , op. cit. States should also consider tasking the Secretariat with preparing a report to evaluate follow-through on the New York Declaration, adopted a year ago, by the beginning of the 82nd General Assembly session in September 2027. The Declaration commits its signatories to a range of measures to end the war in Gaza, to facilitate a credible pathway toward Palestinian self-determination and to support a sovereign Palestinian state living peacefully alongside Israel. 86 “ Endorsement of the New York Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of the Question of Palestine and the Implementation of the Two-State Solution ”, op. cit. Such a report could be useful as the Council considers whether to renew the Board of Peace’s mandate, which it must do by 31 December 2027. Member states could ask the Secretary-General to focus on whether the Board is advancing commitments to reduce civilian suffering, rehabilitate Gaza and preserve a viable political horizon – and whether it is acting consistent with Security Council, General Assembly and International Court of Justice interventions on these matters. While UN members cannot circumvent the deeply flawed ceasefire plan altogether, they can work through the world body to keep a global spotlight on Gaza. It is past time for the General Assembly to recover a sense of urgency for mobilising diplomatic pressure in support of the ceasefire and keeping space open for the Palestinians to pursue self-determination. 4. Reinforcing security and justice support to Haiti International efforts to help restore security in Haiti have reached a decisive phase. The Gang Suppression Force (GSF), a multilateral mission authorised by the Security Council in September 2025 and backed with UN logistical support, landed in Haiti in June. 87 “ Resolution 2793 ”, UNSC S/RES/2793, 30 September 2025. Expected to be at full strength by the end of the year, the force faces the daunting task of confronting armed gangs that have held much of the country hostage for years. 88 Crisis Group Report, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , op. cit.; “ Situation of human rights in Haiti ”, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights A/HRC/61/74, 23 March 2026. International efforts to staff, fund and equip the GSF are essential to ending this painful chapter in Haiti’s history. But even if this force puts gangs on the back foot, it will only be the start of a far longer campaign to bring peace to the country. Haiti’s government and international partners should work closely with the UN to build exit ramps for individuals willing to abandon the gangs and reinforce new judicial bodies to investigate and prosecute gang crimes. The GSF’s close working relationship with the UN could help it avoid the problems that plagued its predecessor, the Kenyan-led Multinational Security Support mission. A new UN support office services the force’s logistics needs (ranging from supplying rations and fuel to covering its medical services and constructing bases) and channels monetary contributions its way. 89 “ Budgets for the periods from 1 October 2025 to 30 June 2026 and from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027 for the United Nations Support Office in Haiti ”, UNGA A/80/630, 10 February 2026. Reasonably predictable funding from the UN’s assessed budget has enabled eight countries to pledge enough troops to surpass the initial target of 5,500 personnel, though as of publication only around 1,200 troops are on the ground. 90 As of publication, the GSF included personnel sent from Chad, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, Mongolia and Sri Lanka. A separate UN trust fund has nearly $226 million in voluntary donations, which have been promised to cover the wages of deployed personnel. 91 As of 30 June, the Trust Fund had $233 million in total pledges, with $184 million in cash receipts. The UN had spent approximately $67 million of the cash receipts leaving $117 million in hand. “ Contributions to the Trust Fund for the Multinational Security Support (MSS) mission for Haiti authorised under SCR 2699 (2023) and Gang Suppression Force (GSF) authorised under SCR 2793 ”, UN, 13 July 2026; “ United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti: Report of the Secretary-General ”, UNSC S/2026/574, 14 July 2026, p. 10. Informal ties also reinforce the force’s partnership with the UN. The Standing Group of Partners, the ad hoc political body with the job of overseeing the mission, appointed UN peacekeeping veterans to the force’s highest ranking civilian and uniformed positions. 92 The Standing Group of Partners includes the U.S., Canada, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, Kenya, and the Bahamas. “ Special representative named for U.S. backed-Gang Suppression Force in Haiti ”, Miami Herald , 2 December 2025; “ UN-appointed anti-gang force commander arrives in Haiti to lead expanded mission ”, Haitian Times , 15 May 2026. These officials are coordinating with senior staff in BINUH, the UN political office in Haiti tasked with engaging Haitian counterparts on governance and human rights, and in the force’s logistics support office. The UN headquarters gave wide-ranging assistance to the force as it went about its technical preparations, including by helping prepare its concept of operations and carry out pre-deployment training. 93 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and UN officials, New York and Port-au-Prince, February, April and June 2026. Difficulties will inevitably arise once the GSF begins going after the gangs in earnest. Civilians are at risk of becoming collateral damage once the mission launches offensives. 94 The Multinational Security Support mission, by contrast, never mustered more than 1,000 police personnel, struggled to secure funding and battled the gangs only alongside the national police. Troop-contributing countries that have taken part in previous UN peacekeeping operations will need to ensure that the soldiers they send to Haiti are prepared for a hostile environment. The Standing Group of Partners and the Security Council should be vigilant in monitoring how the force polices its members’ conduct and metes out any necessary discipline, especially given the history of international personnel committing sexual abuses while serving in Haiti. 95 “ Citing unpunished sex abuse, rights groups urge halt to Sri Lankan troops Haiti deployment ”, The Miami Herald , 28 June 2026. Any gains will be short-lived if Haiti and its partners do not take steps to dismantle the criminal groups for good. Once the force reaches full capacity, member states hope that it can quickly impose a modicum of security. 96 Crisis Group Report, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , op. cit. But any gains will be short-lived if Haiti and its partners do not take steps to dismantle the criminal groups for good. Offering individuals the opportunity to leave the gangs safely, with support for new livelihoods through a program of disarmament, dismantlement and reintegration, will be critical for winding down these groups. 97 The Haitian government and the UN do not use the more common term “demobilisation”, which refers to dissolving non-state armed groups as defined under international humanitarian law. Instead, they refer to “dismantlement”, which envisages individual rather than collective action. “ Letter dated 29 May 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, UNSC S/2026/449, 29 May 2026, p. 3. Important steps have already been taken to this effect. First, in early 2026 Haitian authorities reactivated the National Commission for Disarmament, Dismantlement and Reintegration, which the UN has offered to support in a range of ways. 98 “ Letter dated 29 May 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, UNSC S/2026/449, 29 May 2026. Secondly, the Security Council revised BINUH’s mandate in January to include assisting the state in designing and running a program to find exit ramps for gang members. 99 “ Resolution 2814 ”, UNSC S/RES/2814, 29 January 2026. The UN is also providing technical support to newly established special judicial units, mandated to address complex corruption cases and serious human rights violations, which will also be indispensable to any long-term campaign to weaken the gangs. The hope is that these courts will be able to address the links between powerful actors and criminal activity that have long gone unpunished. The government is working toward providing stronger security protection for the judges taking on these cases, as in the past many have recused themselves after being threatened. 100 In May, the Haitian government launched two specialised judicial units to investigate and prosecute mass crimes, sexual violence and financial crimes, with technical support from the Office of the High Commissioner of Human Rights and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. These units, which are expected to start work soon, could help bring to justice the main perpetrators of crimes committed by gangs, as well as their main supporters. “ United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti: Report of the Secretary-General ”, op. cit., p. 5; Crisis Group telephone interviews, Haitian government and UN officials, July 2025. The focus of the Haitian authorities and their foreign counterparts, understandably, is on combating the gangs by force. But they should simultaneously lay the groundwork for dismantlement that is robust enough to ensure former members are not drawn back into the gangs’ orbit, whether by poverty or the weakness of local security forces. The UN should make sure these long-term objectives do not get lost in the push for tactical victories, particularly because they will require considerably more funding than is now available. 101 Estimates of the needs range from $13.5 million for minimal assistance to over $150 million for a comprehensive suite of DDR and judicial sector programs. “ Letter dated 29 May 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, op. cit. For that reason, donor countries should not just fund the multinational force but also include both dismantlement projects and justice reform in their support to the country. 102 Canadian-French support for establishing two specialised justice units is a model worth replicating. “ Specialised Judicial Units in Haiti ”, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, June 2026. In May, the Secretary-General presented to the Security Council several options for backing disarmament, dismantlement and reintegration initiatives and strengthening Haiti’s judicial system. UN member states have yet to weigh in on which of these options they would be willing to help fund. “ Letter dated 29 May 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, op. cit. 5. Preserving UN operations in the Central African Republic UN peacekeepers have been at the forefront of international efforts to protect civilians and back peace initiatives in the Central African Republic (CAR) since first being dispatched to the country in 2014. The U.S. and China, two of the Council’s permanent members, have suggested that the mission, known as MINUSCA, should now begin preparing to exit, citing the progress the country has made toward stability. (Their own interest is to lower the cost of UN peacekeeping.) Elections held in late December 2025 without a major disruption may bolster their case. 103 Charles Bouëssel, “ Central African Republic: Consolidating Security Gains after the Elections ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 27 January 2026. But when renewing MINUSCA’s mandate in November, diplomats should ensure that the mission retains sufficient capacity to protect civilians and deter armed groups in the country’s troubled east, since it is the only entity that can provide a buffer against worsening instability in that region. MINUSCA continues to fill gaps that the Central African authorities cannot plug. A guarantor of the 2019 peace agreement, the UN mission oversees local peace dialogues and disarmament programs across the country. 104 The Union for Peace in the Central African Republic, Return, Reclamation and Rehabilitation and the Patriotic Movement for the Central African Republic are the most prominent armed groups participating in these disarmament programs. See: “ The Situation in the Central African Republic ”, UNSC S/2026/494, 15 June 2026, paras 8-10. Though CAR’s allies – Rwanda and Russian paramilitaries from the Wagner Group – helped Bangui regain control of towns across the country after a 2021 rebel offensive, MINUSCA is the only external partner tasked with protecting civilians from violence. In many areas outside the capital Bangui, local institutions depend on the mission to build and repair government offices, supply logistical assistance and offer physical protection. The threat of insurgency in CAR is much lower than it was a few years ago, but pockets of insecurity persist along the country’s eastern borders. 105 Bouëssel, “ Central African Republic: Consolidating Security Gains after the Elections ”, op. cit. Fighters from the ex-Séléka rebel coalition, which seized power in 2013 and plunged the country into civil war, as well as allied militias are active in the north east, most recently attacking CAR state forces and UN peacekeepers on 30 June in Am-Dafock, on the Sudan border. 106 “ Central African Republic Situation Report No. 74 as of 30 June, 2026 ”, UN OCHA, 2 July 2026; “ MINUSCA strongly condemns the attack against Am Dafock and the firing targeting the Mission’s base ”, press release, UN OCHA, 30 June 2026. Separately, the Zandé self-defence militia based in Haut-Mbomou prefecture, in the south east, continue to assail civilians and state forces. 107 Crisis Group Africa Report N°319, Central African Republic: Reining in the Zandé Militia , 20 November 2025. UN peacekeepers are often the only force capable of deterring or responding to urgent threats [in the Central African Republic]. Intercommunal violence, opportunistic crime and conflicts between nomadic herders and sedentary farmers remain prevalent nationwide. 108 Crisis Group Africa Report N°317, Violence and Herding in the Central African Republic: Time to Act , 28 May 2025. Women and girls are vulnerable to rape in many places as a result. Spillover from Sudan’s civil war exacerbates these risks: Central African rebels have become war entrepreneurs, providing fighters for both the RSF and the Sudanese army in exchange for money, while over 40,000 Sudanese refugees have fled into north-eastern CAR. UN peacekeepers are often the only force capable of deterring or responding to urgent threats. These developments should give Council members pause when they are considering a drawdown for MINUSCA. In November 2025, the U.S. pushed the Council to task the mission with charting an exit strategy ahead of the mandate renewal, owing in part to their assessment of CAR’s improved conditions and their scepticism about renewing UN operations indefinitely. 109 A draft is expected to be circulated by 15 September. “ Resolution 2800 ”, UNSC S/RES/2800, para 48; “ Central African Republic: Vote on MINUSCA’s Mandate Renewal ”, Security Council Report, 12 November 2025. U.S. and Chinese diplomats have found common cause in lobbying for reductions to the mission’s budget. 110 Crisis Group interviews, UN diplomats, New York, November 2025. See also UN Security Council, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10,041st Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10041, 13 November 2025; “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10,111st Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10041, 25 February 2026; and UN Security Council, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10,181st Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10181, 23 June 2026. Separately, the UN’s liquidity crisis has already forced the mission to repatriate nearly 4,000 troops (more than one quarter of the total) and close 21 operating bases that allowed MINUSCA to intervene in a range of conflict-affected areas outside Bangui. 111 UN leaders used the financial constraints as motivation to reposition MINUSCA personnel in a more mobile posture to get the most out of the smaller footprint. Crisis Group interviews, UN officials, July 2026. Some of the temporary bases had been set up to support the UN’s election assistance to CAR. “ Report of the Secretary-General on the Central African Republic ”, UNSC S/2026/494, 15 June 2026. Though the UN’s financial crisis will make it hard to restore MINUSCA to its mandated strength, Council members should make sure that debates about the mission’s long-term future do not undermine its ability to consolidate the country’s security gains in the short term. In line with the November 2025 resolution, the Central African government and MINUSCA have begun work on a transition plan. A confidential report envisages MINUSCA shifting to a role of strategic support, with some state authority tasks transferable in the short and medium term, while others (notably protection of civilians) remain non-transferable. It also highlights major budgetary challenges Bangui faces in meeting these responsibilities. Diplomats should use the mandate renewal to draw an explicit link between rising insecurity on CAR’s eastern borders, making sure that the mission retains sufficient capacity to conduct operations in that part of the country. They should also encourage MINUSCA to make non-military efforts to prevent further escalation through local political dialogues followed by various forms of disarmament. Council members should ensure that MINUSCA’s leadership is working closely with UN envoys in the Horn of Africa to better anticipate and react to any spillover from Sudan’s war. All Security Council members acknowledge MINUSCA’s importance in helping CAR achieve a degree of stability through protecting civilians, restoring public services and supporting political dialogue, even if they continue to debate when and how those parts of its work should be whittled down. For the moment, the Council should help CAR consolidate gains rather than push for a hasty downsizing that would generate risks in a country where the UN has already invested heavily for the past decade. 6. Rallying around the International Criminal Court The Trump administration’s “sweeping campaign” to dismantle the International Criminal Court (ICC), announced in July, is the latest salvo in its assault upon the international order. 112 The campaign reportedly includes highlighting the court’s harms through high-level diplomatic outreach, threats to revisit U.S. assistance if states do not reject the Court’s ability to prosecute U.S. officials, visa revocations, travel bans and additional sanctions on ICC personnel. “ State Department Launches Campaign to Dismantle International Criminal Court’s Threat to American Sovereignty ”, U.S. Department of State, 13 July 2026; Victor Jack, “ US pressures NATO allies to destroy International Criminal Court ”, Politico , 9 September 2026. It is not the first time that the U.S. has openly clashed with the ICC or sanctioned its personnel. 113 As of publication, “nine of the eighteen Judges, both of the two Deputy-Prosecutors, the former Prosecutor and one staff member have been sanctioned by the United States”. See “ The ICC strongly rejects new US sanctions designations ”, press release, International Criminal Court, 19 August 2026. But its latest move to obstruct the Court’s work by sanctioning its president and threatening its member state backers is a regrettable escalation that risks setting a precedent for U.S. efforts to bend other parts of the multilateral system to its will. A number of the UN’s most powerful member states (including the U.S., Russia and China) never joined the Court and generally resist its efforts in situations where they have deemed interests, member states that do back the court can chart their own course. Those that have not already done so should make clear their continued support for a strong, independent ICC, noting its role as the only permanent tribunal mandated to pursue individual accountability for international crimes, including those linked to conflict. The current schism between the U.S. and the ICC is the latest episode in what has been a rollercoaster relationship. 114 Stephen Pomper, “ The International Criminal Court’s Case against the United States in Afghanistan ”, Just Security , 13 November 2017. The U.S. never ratified the Rome Statute – the treaty establishing the ICC – even though it played a central role in negotiating the text and signed the document. Washington has long worried that the Court would prosecute U.S. servicemembers for their conduct abroad. In the early years of the Court, the George W. Bush administration purported to “un-sign” the treaty and pressured ICC member states to pledge they would not hand over U.S. personnel to the Court. Though the U.S. later cooperated closely with the ICC in some matters, the prosecutor’s decision in 2017 to investigate the conduct of international forces deployed to Afghanistan prompted the first Trump White House to place certain Court officers under sanctions. 115 For example, the Bush and Barack Obama administrations supported cases involving situations in the DRC and Sudan, and the Biden administration provided evidence to the Court regarding alleged Russian war crimes in Ukraine. Stephen Pomper, “ The US and ICC May Still Steer Past Each Other – Why and How ”, Just Security , 5 April 2018. The Biden administration lifted those, several months before the ICC prosecutor announced that he would “deprioritise” work in Afghanistan that was unrelated to the Taliban. 116 Nahal Toosi, “ Biden lifts sanctions on International Criminal Court officials ”, Politico , 2 April 2021; “ Statement of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, Karim A. A. Khan QC, following the application for an expedited order under article 18(2) seeking authorisation to resume investigations in the Situation in Afghanistan ”, press release, International Criminal Court, 27 September 2021.
